headline: New Haven Breakwall Porgies Keep the Rod Bent While Blues Sneak Back In
subhead: Green crabs and hi-lo rigs are filling coolers on the rockpiles while sea bass hold deep and stripers slip into a dawn-only pattern.
body_markdown:
Dropped a hi-lo rig baited with green crab off the outer breakwall Tuesday morning, right on the last hour of the flood, and had a double-header of porgies before my coffee went cold. That's the story of the season out here — you can set your watch by it. The scup are stacked on every rockpile from the New Haven Harbor breakwalls out to Charles Island, and they haven't cared one bit about the heat that's been sitting on top of this Sound for weeks.

The pattern right now is almost boringly reliable, which I say as a compliment. Anchor up tight to the breakwall rocks in 15 to 20 feet, or work the north side of Charles Island where the bar drops into deeper water, and a hi-lo with size 6 or 8 hooks tipped with green crab or squid strips is going to put porgies in the bucket on just about any tide stage. I like the last two hours of the flood into the top — current's still moving enough to keep bait scent working but it's not ripping you off the spot. Fish are running 8 to 12 inches with a scattering of chunky 13s mixed in, plenty big enough to fry up that night.

When you want a bigger tug, drop down to the deeper structure. Falkner Island's rockpiles and the edges of Stratford Shoal are holding black sea bass in 30 to 40 feet, and they've been the bonus fish all month — a nice change of pace from the porgy grind. Squid strips or a small piece of clam on the bottom hook of that same hi-lo rig works fine, but if you want to target sea bass specifically, jig a diamond jig or a bucktail tipped with Gulp right on bottom and hop it slow. They're not shy about eating right now, and a handful of keepers in the 14 to 16 inch range is a normal trip out there this week.

Fluke are the frustrating piece of the puzzle. Milford Gulf has been giving up drifts full of short fluke — plenty of bites, not much filling the cooler. That warm water sitting on top of the Sound has them lazy and undersized, the same story playing out across the whole basin right now. If you're set on a keeper, I'd fish the deeper edges of the Gulf on the outgoing where there's a little more current and cooler water pushing through, and stick with bigger baits — a whole strip of squid or a 5-inch Gulp swimming mullet on a bucktail — to weed out the dinks.

Stripers have gone quiet in the middle of the day, which isn't a surprise with the Sound running warm — we're talking mid-70s pushing toward 80 in the shallows. That compresses the bite into a tight window right at first light. I've been sliding out to the sandbar off Charles Island before sunrise, working a topwater popper or a soft-plastic swimbait along the drop where the bar falls into deeper water, and connecting with slot fish for about 45 minutes before the sun gets high and they slide off into deeper, cooler water. Same story off the Hammonasset flats — dawn is the whole show right now, and once that sun's up, you're better off switching to bottom fishing.

Here's the piece I'll flag because we called it a couple weeks back — said the bluefish resurgence would spread east from the Western Sound reef structure while porgy held as the anchor bite, and that's exactly what's playing out. Snapper blues have been thick in the harbor and around the breakwall pilings, snapping up small metals and Kastmasters, and I've started seeing a few adult-class blues, 3 to 4 pounds, mixing into the porgy spots off Charles Island. That's a good sign for late August — those adult blues tend to build right through Labor Day once the bait gets moving, and having them show up on structure alongside the porgies gives you a real one-two punch on a single anchor spot.

Worth mentioning: we've had that typical August pattern of afternoon thunderstorms rolling through, and I've had some of my best striper and bluefish action in that short window right after a front pushes through — the air pressure drops, the bait gets nervous, and fish that have been sulking in the heat turn on for twenty or thirty minutes. If you see those clouds building out toward Long Island in the afternoon, don't pack it in. Get your gear stowed, ride it out, and be ready to fish that first clearing.

Looking ahead, tidal flow is starting to build back up as we push toward the August 28 full moon, and that should sharpen everything — more current means more bait pinned against structure, which means better sea bass and porgy action and a real shot at extending that striper window past dawn. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd hit the Charles Island bar at first light for stripers, then slide over to the breakwall rockpiles once the sun's up and let the porgies do the rest of the work.
